crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Clustering papers by meaning groups research articles according to their semantic content rather than surface keywords or citation links alone. It supports literature review, research gap analysis, and citation mapping by revealing thematic clusters across a corpus. The practice is used in bibliometrics, systematic review, and discovery interfaces where a reader needs to move from a single paper to a body of related work. It treats a paper as a unit of meaning, usually represented by its title, abstract, or full text.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard research computing infrastructure, from a single workstation to a cloud instance with a GPU for embedding large corpora. A typical pipeline stores paper text and metadata in a document store or relational database, then computes vector embeddings with a pretrained language model. Those vectors are indexed in a vector database or an in memory matrix for similarity search and clustering. For a small library, such as a few hundred papers, CPU only processing is usually sufficient.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method begins by converting each paper into a dense vector, often using an embedding model trained on scientific text, so that papers with similar claims or methods sit close together in vector space. Dimensionality reduction, such as UMAP, is then applied to make the high dimensional vectors tractable and to preserve local neighbourhoods. A clustering step, commonly HDBSCAN or k means, assigns papers to groups, and each cluster is labelled by its most frequent terms or by a short generated summary. The result is a map where distance reflects semantic similarity, not citation count or journal.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on text reuse, model bias, and provenance. Clustering relies on abstracts or full texts that may be paywalled, so a working system should store only what a licence allows and link to the original paper rather than reproduce long excerpts. The clusters themselves can inherit bias from the embedding model, for example by separating work along subfield jargon rather than true conceptual difference. Provenance matters because a cluster is a derived artefact, and any claim about what a group of papers means should trace back to the source documents and the model version used.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward retrieval augmented discovery, where a reader asks a question and the system returns not just a ranked list but a labelled cluster of papers that answer different parts of the question. Embeddings are becoming better at capturing argument structure and experimental claims, not just topic similarity. Future tools may cluster papers by method, dataset, or finding rather than by broad subject, and update clusters as new preprints appear. The goal is a living map of a research area that a working scientist can read without needing to understand the underlying vectors.
